planting.note: Plant container stock in late fall or early winter; irrigate regularly only through the first one to two seasons, then cut summer water sharply, since mature-plant summer irrigation invites root rot.

directions: A cold-hardy, upright-mounding evergreen from Sierra and Klamath elevations, this manzanita handles far colder winters than coastal species, giving mountain-climate gardeners a true manzanita option with year-round structure and bronze-red bark. Plant in decomposed-granite or other fast-draining, non-alkaline soil. Because manzanita roots resent disturbance, grow nursery stock to a healthy size and transplant in late fall or early winter rather than moving young plants repeatedly.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into medium-to-slow-draining soil, including clay; limit irrigation to twice monthly in summer once established.

directions: A North Coast Ranges endemic valued for especially attractive shreddy red bark and showy pink-to-white spring flower clusters, this manzanita tolerates serpentine and clay soils where many natives struggle, and takes pruning well enough to be hedged. If shaping as a hedge, prune in late summer rather than after rains to avoid fungal branch dieback entering fresh cuts, and sterilize shears between cuts, since manzanitas are broadly susceptible to a common bark pathogen.

planting.note: Plant rooted softwood cuttings in fall into sandy or beach-sand soil; hold summer irrigation to at most twice a month once established.

directions: Only a named cultivar of this species was previously represented in this dataset — the plain bare species is a low, mat-forming coastal manzanita prized for red-edged new growth and dense white-to-pale-pink flower clusters, fast-growing by manzanita standards and excellent for bank stabilization or groundcover. It is unusually tolerant of clay and adobe for a manzanita as long as water never stands on the crown. Prune selectively to remove dead wood or reveal branch structure rather than for size control, sterilizing tools between cuts.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into well-drained forest or chaparral-type soil in full sun to light shade; avoid overhead summer watering once roots are established.

directions: Distinctive woolly, felted gray-green foliage sets this manzanita apart visually from the glossy-leaved species already in the dataset, with a long bloom window from winter through summer and a form ranging from matted groundcover to a spreading shrub. Its woolly leaf surface helps it handle more summer heat reflection than smooth-leaved relatives, but it still needs excellent drainage to avoid root rot. Because growth habit ranges from prostrate mats to upright spreaders depending on provenance, check the specific population before siting it as a groundcover versus a specimen shrub.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into deep, high-organic-content, slightly acidic woodland soil, a departure from the lean decomposed granite most manzanitas prefer; give it room to reach its larger potential size before crowding.

directions: Striking small, round, glossy leaves and red bark give this manzanita a reach into small-tree scale where conditions suit, with nearly year-round bloom from winter through fall in cool, foggy coastal gardens. It performs best replicating its native cool, foggy coastal or coniferous-woodland habitat and can struggle inland without that fog influence. This is a strong choice for Northern California maritime climates underrepresented among the chaparral-adapted manzanitas already in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated cuttings in fall into fast, medium, or slow-draining sandy soil; give some afternoon shade in hotter inland gardens and never let salt spray hit the foliage directly.

directions: A rare, petite, flat-to-creeping Monterey-area endemic that forms low mats in pure sand, this manzanita is valuable as a specialty groundcover for sandy coastal gardens where most manzanitas, which demand rocky or granitic drainage, don't naturally fit. It is adapted to Monterey's cool maritime climate and is one of the more clay-tolerant manzanitas, but never let salt spray hit the foliage directly. Because it's rare and endangered in the wild, source only from reputable native-plant nurseries rather than wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall and decide early whether to prune for groundcover or allow mounding to specimen-shrub scale; reddish new growth is most vivid with full sun.

directions: A Monterey County endemic combining reddish new growth with an unusually long winter bloom period of pink-to-white flowers, this manzanita can be pruned to stay low as groundcover or left to mound into a large shrub, giving one species two very different landscape uses. Unlike most manzanitas, its form is genuinely shapeable by pruning choice rather than fixed by genetics. The reddish new growth is most vivid in full sun; partial shade mutes the color contrast.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated cuttings in fall into coarse, well-drained soil such as decomposed granite, matching its native stony-slope or volcanic-outcrop habitat.

directions: A San Diego County and Otay Mountains endemic with light-pink new foliage maturing to gray-green and an early, long-lasting white bloom, this manzanita is a southern, warm-chaparral counterpart to the mostly central and northern California species already in the dataset, and usable as a hedge. Ordinary garden loam without amendment will hold too much moisture around the roots, so coarse, well-drained soil is essential. As a San Diego-area rarity, source nursery-propagated stock rather than wild material.
